chapter_theme: Valmiki's sixteen verses call themselves the key to all the Siddhars' songs. The letter that is formless-with-form is the cosmos and the body; what comes and goes is the breath (vaasi), which is the sun and moon, the father and mother, and the four Saiva paths folded into one inhalation, retention and release. Against this the poet sets the many who read big books, melt before stone gods, wear matted hair, tiger skin and ash, build Vedas, puranas and castes in their own languages for a living, and howl in the forest without knowing the cause. The method is brief: the middle street from the perineum to the crown, silence, the mind kept where the breath arises, a guarded diet and daily duty; the secret is not to be shown to fools.
structure_note: 2469 to 2471 set the doctrine (letter, body as cosmos, breath as the paths); 2472 to 2478 attack the counterfeit forms of the four paths, of guruhood, of garb and of scripture and caste, closing on the one who sees Siva at the nose-tip; 2479 to 2484 give the key itself: the author's claim, the body's middle way, the two breaths, the sight without witness, diet, and the breath as the one need.

2469.reading: Praising the feet of Siva, who stands as darkness turned to light, the poet promises to expound the letter: what stands formless-with-form is the letter, it is beginning and end, cosmos and body; the form that stands as sun and moon is the form of Siva-Shakti and of Vishnu; and he tells the hearer to set the mind on what came and what went.
2469.nuance: எழுத்து (the letter) is not named; tradition hears the pranava or the first letter அ. வந்ததிலும் போனதிலும் (in what came and what went) is explained by the next verse as the in- and out-breath, so the whole opening resolves into breath. ரவிமதி (sun and moon) is a coded pair the Siddhars use for the two breaths or the two nostrils; the verse leaves it as a form of the gods.

2470.reading: What comes and goes is the vaasi, and the sun and moon in the sky are the vaasi; the one of clear mind is the siddha, and the one who knows the whole world as Siva is the siddha; Nandi the mount is the gross body, four-faced Brahma is eye, nose, ear and tongue, the elephant-faced is the holy breath of Siva-Shakti; know the sun and moon as father and mother.
2470.nuance: The verse is an allegory key: each god is a part of the body or of breathing. Which breath Ganapati (தந்திமுகன்) stands for, and whether father and mother are the right and left breaths, is tradition's reading, not the verse's statement. The definition of the siddha as one who sees all as Siva is plain and carries no cipher.

2471.reading: Inhalation (pooraka) is the path of chariyai, retention (kumbaka) that subsides is kiriyai, exhalation (resaka) that parts is yoga, and what stands without slipping is jnana; the prana-air that turns and enters the body is the house in which great Siva-Shakti comes to rest; the one who joins it with a clear mind is the siddha and may be called Siva himself.
2471.nuance: The four Saiva paths, elsewhere stages of a life or classes of practitioner, are here phases of one breath, and the fourth is the breath held still. வீடு in line 6 can be read as 'house' or as release; the breath's resting place is both.

2472.reading: In the world those who have read the great books call all they have seen 'charitai'; they melt before stone and copper, call them god, worship them and call that kiriyai; calling it yoga they eat fruit and roots and wander like mutes; and saying 'jnana' they split hairs and go round like a crow-mad beast.
2472.nuance: The verse is the counterfeit of 2471: each of the four paths as practised. சரிதை is probably சரியை (chariyai) bent to the rhyme, though it can also mean 'history', what they have seen written down. காக்கைபித்தன் (crow-madman) is obscure; the drift of the line is clear.

2473.reading: Some few in the world, poring over the great books, hold forth; to make a living they put many costumes on the body and roam, call themselves gurus and others disciples, slyly give initiation and call others evil, and shout that they themselves are the holy Trimurti: dregs who do not know the cause.
2473.nuance: தூடிப்பார் and தெற்றுவார் are uncertain words; the first is probably 'flaunt' and the second 'deceive'. The charge is economic as much as doctrinal: the guru-disciple relation and initiation are a trade (பிழைக்க, to make a living), a theme that returns in 2476.

2474.reading: Some in the world put on matted hair, tiger skin, ochre robe and bead strings, smear the whole fleshy body with ash and call themselves yogis and jnanis; they call Siva worship and initiation honey, say they have seen Vishnu with their own eyes, and crores of them roam the forest howling, not knowing the cause.
2474.nuance: The verse does not say ash or garb are wrong; it says they are worn without knowing the cause (காரணம்), the word on which the next verse turns. The forest-roaming yogi, elsewhere the ideal, is here the type of the lost.

2475.reading: Those who howl are crores upon crores; those who have seen the cause are few; those who hold to the Supreme and have seen are a handful; the many in the world do not know within themselves the kala that rose; so do not scatter like the scattered, but when Siva-Shakti comes, stand in yourself.
2475.nuance: The verbs பதறு, உதறு, சிதறு are chosen for the rhyme and their subjects are loose. உதித்த கலை (the kala that rose) is taken by tradition as the breath, or the inner moon's digit; and 'when Siva-Shakti comes' as the moment of the breath's rising (compare 2470, where Siva-Shakti is the holy breath).

2476.reading: In the language of the great ones who said 'stand', within the wide world they built the four Vedas, the six shastras and the eighteen puranas that fill the belly, and Vedantas that dissolve stones, each in his own language; and in the old world they strung together the four castes and the many castes, each so as to make a living.
2476.nuance: Scripture, sect and caste are treated alike as human constructions made for livelihood (வயிறு பிழை, பிழைக்க). The next verse softens this: embodied beings need a language, and the secret book came from Siva and Sivakami. 'Vedantas that dissolve stones' may praise their power or mock their pretension.

2477.reading: Were there no 'I' in the world they would perish by their own greatness and fall into the world; but one who takes a body of flesh needs everything, and in the world each needs his own language; deer-eyed Sivakami and Siva together looked at the faces of the great sages and spoke the secret book, and by honey-like Sivakami's grace they gathered many crores of the languages of lands.
2477.nuance: The first two lines are hard: தான் may be the ego or the self, and the sense may be that without self-assertion the world's builders would fall. What is clear is the concession: after 2476's attack, language and scripture are granted a divine source and a bodily necessity.

2478.reading: Those who have studied languages hold forth confidently without knowing the language of the land; they praise all they see, meet a wonder and forget; the stubborn grandees who do not know the vaasi bewilder with words and have no method; but those who have seen Siva in the middle of the nose-tip are themselves Brahma, Vishnu and Siva.
2478.nuance: நாசிநுனி (nose-tip) is where the breath is felt and where the yogic gaze is fixed; tradition takes seeing Siva there as the breath-practice itself. சண்டி மாண்பர் is an uncertain phrase, probably 'obstinate worthies'. The verse ends the attack on words with a place in the body.

2479.reading: The key to the songs of all the eighteen is Valmiki's sixteen; the siddhas who had reached Siva all looked at my book and complained to Siva, and the Lord was angry; so that it not go to waste, by Siva's permission and grace I opened and told it for the world: within the nine planets, the tongue, mouth, ear and nose, beyond the middle.
2479.nuance: பதினெண் பேர் are the eighteen siddhars, and பதினாறு this work's sixteen verses: the poem claims to be the cipher key to the corpus. நவக்கிரகம் (nine planets) within the body is taken by tradition as the nine openings; the verse only lists four organs and points beyond their middle, continued in the next verse.

2480.reading: Beyond the middle of tongue, mouth, ear and nose runs the middle street from the perineum to the crown: strike there, saying 'there', and butt at it; worship the Mother and recite the Veda; with speech unmoving, taking silence, keep the mind at the place where the vaasi arises; then the mind, entering with the vaasi, is removed, and you will see the order in which it subsides into thought.
2480.nuance: நடுவீதி (middle street) from குய்யம் to உச்சி is the central channel without its name. The instruction is in cipher ('strike', 'butt'), and the last two lines are syntactically loose; the plain point is that mind and breath are to be held together at the breath's source.

2481.reading: Hard for anyone to see the two breaths; the one who sees them is the Siva-siddha; hard to attain, but if this book is got one may be called a siddha of the earth; hard to see, the holy breath of Siva-Shakti; do not show this book to fools; hard to appear, the dizziness of the eyes simply passes; I have told the subtlety that is hard to tell.
2481.nuance: இருசுவாசம் (two breaths) is the in- and out-breath, or in tradition the sun and moon breaths of the two nostrils. விழிமயக்கம் சும்மாப்போம் may mean that the practice ends the eyes' bewilderment, or that the eyes' delusion is all that leaves.

2482.reading: The poet tells the book's subtlety so that the vaasi may be seen; the subtle of subtles cannot be renounced; there is no witness, no companion, no hearsay and no doubt; the sight is like dwelling in the wishing-tree; having seen the cause with the eye, he saw Umai who gives rule just so, and the conduct of the dance of bliss is the guard.
2482.nuance: சாட்சியில்லை துணையில்லை கேள்வியில்லை (no witness, no companion, no hearsay) is the poem's claim against book-learning: the seeing needs no authority. விழியைக் காண (to see the eye) is obscure; it may mean seeing with the inner eye. The last line's syntax is uncertain.

2483.reading: Hear the diet for guarding it: eat fruits, the five juices and the finest foods in due measure and guard Siva; my son, read the siddhas' guru-book; the soul must suffer no decay; each must perform his daily duties; for those who stand firm comes vaasi-siddhi, and the sixteen bear fruit with distinction.
2483.nuance: After mocking rite in 2472, the verse keeps நித்யகர்மம் (daily duty) as a condition of the practice, and adds diet and the study of a guru-text: the attack was on rite without the cause, not on rite. பதினாறு is again the sixteen verses, or the sixteen kalas of the moon in the yogic reading.

2484.reading: To be He oneself, vaasi is needed, and a place to stand within oneself is needed; for all who stand as the sky-dweller there is siddhi, and when the mind is in the sky it is seen like the moon; for the siddhas who are honey, the herb that never cloys is the head, the seat of the body; I have told the sign so that you may be king, and on earth the sixteen draw to a close.
2484.nuance: தெவிட்டா மூலி (the herb that never cloys) is the head: the siddhas' medicine is in the body, not in a plant, a reading tradition supports and the verse half-states. வானுக்குள் மனம் (mind in the sky) is the inner space of the head; மதிபோல் can be 'like the moon' or 'like intellect'. குறுகத் தானே may mean the sixteen verses end here, or that the sixteen kalas contract.

links.note: Tirumular gives puraka, kumbhaka and recaka their measures; Valmiki keeps the three terms and maps them onto the four Saiva paths, so that the whole of Saiva practice is one breath.

Tirumular sorts the four paths into four kinds of people, with the siddhas at jnana; Valmiki makes them four phases of one breath that every practitioner passes through, and the siddha is the one who joins them.
Sivavakkiyar maps the four paths onto the four states of release; Valmiki maps the same four onto inhalation, retention, exhalation and stillness.
The Kural's hunter hiding in a bush is Valmiki's fruit-eating mute who calls his wandering yoga: austerity worn as cover for what is not austerity.
Tirumular's fools in guises who dance, sing and wail yet never see Siva's feet are Valmiki's book-readers who melt before stone, eat roots and go round like beasts.
Both name the false guru by his trade: Tirumular's has surveyed mantra and yoga yet goes blind for food; Valmiki's dons costumes, takes disciples and gives initiation to make a living.
The Kural's cow grazing in a tiger's skin; Valmiki's yogi in matted hair, tiger skin and ash who does not know the cause. The skin marks the pretence in both.
Tirumular wants the king to test those who put on matted hair, tuft and thread and act the wise; Valmiki counts them in crores howling in the forest. Both make the garb empty without knowledge.

Agasthiyar counts both the unseeing wanderers and those who know the cause as crores upon crores; Valmiki, in the same words, says those who have seen the cause are few. On a plain reading of Agasthiyar's second line the counts conflict; it may be hyperbole or a corrupt line.

Sivavakkiyar asks what caste is when all water is one and the five elements are one; Valmiki says the four castes and the many castes were strung together by men for a living. Both deny caste a natural ground.

The Kural says birth is alike for all and distinction comes from work; Valmiki says caste was made by men to live by. Both refuse birth as a ground of rank, though the Kural keeps a ground in deeds that Valmiki does not mention.

Tirumular: fix both gazes at the middle of the nose and we become Siva. Valmiki: those who have seen Siva at the nose-tip are themselves the three gods. The same place in the body yields the same identity.
Mounachiddhar knows the gaze by the way of the nose-tip and the raising of the vaasi; Valmiki sets seeing Siva at the nose-tip against the word-mongers who do not know the vaasi.
Tirumular: where the abiding mind is, there the breath is. Valmiki: keep the mind at the place where the vaasi arises and the mind enters with it and subsides.

Tirumular says no one knows the measure of the breath drawn in and let out through both nostrils, and that those who know it kick Death; Valmiki says the two breaths are hard for anyone to see and the one who sees them is the Siva-siddha.
Tirumular's Lord tells the secret of release only to those on the path of virtue; Valmiki forbids showing his book to fools. Both guard the teaching by the fitness of the hearer.

The Kural makes understanding the seeing of the true substance of whatever is heard; Valmiki's seeing needs no witness, companion or hearsay. Both place knowledge in direct seeing rather than in report, and Valmiki goes further in dismissing report.
Tirumular stayed through the ages keeping a measured diet with mind withdrawn; Valmiki prescribes fruit, the five juices and fine foods in due measure as the guard of the breath-practice.

source_issues: 2473: தூடிப்பா ருலகத்தல் has a dropped vowel (உலகத்தில்); தூடிப்பார் itself is an uncertain word.
2477: மாமுனிர் is probably மாமுனிவர்; the line is one syllable short.
